newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices firm as Iraq jars traders' nerves.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices firm as Iraq jars traders' nerves.

text.p: Oil prices firmed on Tuesday as jumpy traders assessed the impact of continuing tension in Iraq which has sent prices soaring towards their highest levels since the Gulf War.

World benchmark Brent Blend crude oil from the North Sea ended the day at $22.88 a barrel for the October contract on London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE), 27 cents up from Monday. It had sunk to $22.32 early in the day.
U.S. officials denied Iraqi claims they had fired three missiles at U.S. aircraft in southern Iraq but the uncertainty added to traders' nervousness.
"We have warned Saddam Hussein that we retain the right and will, in fact, take actions necessary to protect our pilots," a U.S. Pentagon spokesman said.
Charles Gray of Prudential Bache said: "Traders are getting spooked on any sort of story."
But IPE brokers said much of the upward move on Tuesday was in response to technical patterns on the historical price charts.
They said that when dealers saw in the morning the October Brent contract test, but fail to break though, Monday's low point of $22.31, they took that as a signal to buy.
"It was a classic bounce," said one broker.
Support then weighed in from across the Atlantic, where the October crude oil contract on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) broke through the important psychological level of $24.00 a barrel.
Prices spiked up by around a dollar last week after Iraqi troops moved into Iraqi Kurdistan in support of a Kurdish faction, drawing U.S. retaliatory attacks against targets in the south of Iraq.

Iraq, whose exports have been under a United Nations embargo since it invaded Kuwait in August 1990, was to have been allowed a limited renewable oil sale, worth $2 billion over six months, to pay for essential food and medicines.
The latest military activity prompted the U.N. to suspend the deal.
In anticipation of resumed Iraqi oil sales some refineries had allowed their stocks to run low and subsequently had to scramble to cover requirements at higher prices.
Since then the market has been consolidating at new higher levels and waiting for any fresh news out of the Middle East.
Prices have also been supported by renewed demand for gas oil (heating oil) ahead of the northern hemisphere winter.

With analysts fearing that low stocks of heating oil in both the United States and Europe might fall short of meeting winter demand, a close eye will be kept on heating stocks data out of the United States later on Wednesday.
"Without a build in heating oil, prices are likely to rise," said GNI in its daily energy report.
